title: Blades explained: wood, carbon, speed and handles
seo_title: Table tennis blades explained: wood, carbon, handles
description: How table tennis blades work: plies of wood, carbon and other fibres, inner and outer fibre, speed ratings, weight, handle shapes and what to buy.
summary: The blade decides how fast and how firm your bat feels. Here is how plies, carbon layers and handles change it, and which kind to pick as you improve.
key_points: The blade is the bat without its rubbers; at least 85% of its thickness must be natural wood.
Most blades are five or seven layers (plies) of wood, and many add two thin layers of carbon or another fibre.
Fibre just under the surface (outer fibre) plays faster; fibre near the core (inner fibre) holds the ball a little longer.
Handles come in flared, straight and anatomic shapes for the shakehand grip, and shorter shapes for penhold.
Start on an allround all-wood blade and move to a faster or fibre blade once your strokes are reliable.
body: The blade is the wooden part of a bat: the head and the handle, before any rubber goes on. Blades differ in how fast the ball comes off them, how firm they feel, how much they weigh and the shape of the handle. Those differences come mainly from how many layers of wood they have, whether layers of carbon or another fibre are added, and where those layers sit. For your first year, an allround blade made only of wood is the right choice.
## What the rules allow

The ITTF, the world governing body, gives blades a lot of freedom. Under Law 2.4 a racket may be any size, shape or weight, but the blade must be flat and rigid. At least 85% of the blade's thickness must be natural wood. The glue layers inside it may be reinforced with a fibrous material such as carbon fibre, glass fibre or compressed paper, but any such layer may be no thicker than 7.5% of the total thickness or 0.35mm, whichever is smaller. That is why even the most high-tech blades are mostly wood.
## Plies: the layers of wood

A blade is built from thin sheets of wood glued together, called plies. Many blades have five plies. Butterfly's Petr Korbel blade, for example, is five plies of wood, 5.9mm thick and weighs 90g on average. Its Korbel SK7 adds two more plies of wood, making it 6.8mm thick and 92g.

To help players compare, Butterfly publishes two figures for each blade. The reaction property is, in its words, "the quantified value illustrating the base speed of a blade": the higher the number, the faster the ball leaves the blade. The vibration property describes the feel at impact; a high figure means a blade with a harder touch. The numbers are Butterfly's own and are useful for comparing its blades with each other rather than with other brands.
## Carbon and other fibres

Many faster blades add two thin layers of synthetic fibre to the wood. Butterfly's best-known example is the Viscaria, built from five plies of wood and two layers of Arylate-Carbon (ALC), a woven mix of two fibres that Butterfly describes as popular for its "flexibility, usability, and moderate bounce". The Viscaria is 5.8mm thick and has a reaction figure of 11.8. A later version with Super ALC, which weaves in more fibre for a higher bounce, rates 12.1.

Other fibres appear in blade descriptions too: ZLC (Butterfly's ZL Carbon), Tamca 5000 in the Primorac Carbon, and plain carbon or glass fibre from other makers. They all work within the same 7.5% rule.
## Outer fibre and inner fibre

Where the fibre sits matters as much as what it is. In an outer-fibre blade the fibre layers lie just beneath the surface veneer, the traditional design. Butterfly says this enhances the feel of the fibre "enabling faster shots". In an inner-fibre blade, a design Butterfly introduced in 2009, the fibre sits next to the wooden core, which the company says gives "a touch of longer dwell time": the ball stays on the bat a fraction longer, so it is easier to control.

The difference shows in the numbers. Butterfly's Innerforce Layer ALC uses the same five plies plus two ALC layers as the Viscaria, but with the fibre on the inside; its reaction figure is 10.7, against 11.8 for the outer-fibre Viscaria.
## Speed classes

Manufacturers sort blades by the style they suit, from defensive blades for choppers (players who defend far from the table with backspin), through allround blades, to offensive ones. Butterfly's own specification table groups its shakehand blades as defensive, all-round and offensive. Labels differ between brands and there is no common scale, so compare blades within one maker's range, and treat "offensive" on any blade as a warning for a beginner.
## Weight

Most blades weigh somewhere between the high 70s and low 90s of grams. Butterfly's averages run from 77g for the five-ply Boll Mezzoforte to 92g for the seven-ply Korbel SK7. Wood is a natural material, and Butterfly notes that the weight of a blade varies with humidity and temperature, so two copies of the same model can differ by several grams. Remember that two rubbers will add a good deal more; our guide to [sponge thickness and hardness](/guide/rubber-sponge-thickness-hardness.html) explains how thicker sponge adds weight.
## Handle shapes

For the shakehand grip, the way most players hold the bat, there are three common handles. A flared handle (FL) widens towards the end, which helps it stay in the hand. A straight handle (ST) is the same width all the way down. An anatomic handle (AN) bulges in the middle to fill the palm. On the Viscaria, Butterfly's flared handle is 100mm long and 34mm wide at the end, and the straight one is 28mm wide at the end.

Penhold players, who grip the bat like a pen, use shorter handles. Butterfly's Chinese penhold (CS) version of the Viscaria Super ALC has an 82mm handle. Our guide to [penhold and shakehand grips](/guide/penhold-vs-shakehand-grip.html) explains the two grips.
## What to buy at each stage

As a beginner, use an allround blade made only of wood, usually as part of a ready-made bat; our guide to [what bat to buy](/guide/what-table-tennis-bat-to-buy.html) covers that first step. Once you play every week and can loop (play a heavy topspin stroke) consistently, a faster all-wood offensive blade or an inner-fibre blade is a sensible next step. Butterfly describes the outer-fibre Viscaria as tailored to attack with an emphasis on spin; blades like it make little sense until your technique is secure.

Whatever you choose, the rubbers you put on it will change the bat as much as the blade does. Read [rubbers explained](/guide/table-tennis-rubbers-explained.html) next, then [custom or ready-made bats](/guide/custom-vs-ready-made-bats.html) when you are ready to build your own.
